newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong gamblers pile "red chips" on China.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong gamblers pile "red chips" on China.

text.p: On the last frenetic day of stock market trading of colonial rule, Hong Kong investors on Friday piled up "red chips" in a gamble on their future prosperity under communist China.
As Scottish bagpipers lamented the close of the last major colonial outpost, the territory's residents were furiously putting their money on Beijing-backed businesses.

"Red chip" companies -- seen as big winners in the "one country, two systems" deal that permits Hong Kong's freewheeling capitalism to continue -- soared with three full days to go before the colony returns to China on Monday midnight.

The stock market was well above the psychological 15,000 level in Friday morning's session and red chips rose four percent on handover optimism. After closing on Friday night, it will be on on holiday until Thursday.
Investors swept aside a political wrangle pitting pro-democracy leaders against the departing British, focusing instead on Hong Kong's great passion -- making money.
"Sentiment is strong and people are aggressively participating in the market ahead of the handover," said Ben Kwong, director of research at Dharmala Securities.

Charges of "perfidious Albion" have been flying, with democracy activists accusing Britain of a sell-out over its decision to follow the lead of the United States and send its Hong Kong envoy to the swearing-in of the new Beijing-picked legislature.
Governor Chris Patten stepped into the row on Friday, insisting Britain had a moral responsibility to maintain links with the government that would run Hong Kong.
The provisional legislature, to be sworn in shortly after the handover, replaces a democratically elected body.
Patten, the last governor in 156 years of British colonial rule, did not directly answer when asked why Britain initially took a strong stand against attending and then changed tack.
He told a radio call-in programme there was a distinction between sending working-level officials and Prime Minister Tony Blair, who will skip the event.
There was no way a British government could justify to its parliament "publicly elected officials going to the inauguration of a provisional legislature which is not elected".
"It's not a question of a boycott, it's a question of what is right and seemly and what is not right," he said.

Martin Lee, head of the Democratic Party and by most polls even more popular than Beijing's chosen Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa, sounded a pessimistic note. He and other democrats will be excluded from the new chamber.
"There is apprehension now as to the possible, and even very likely, loss of some of our freedoms," he told Cable News Network (CNN).
As he strode into the Legislative Council for what was likely to be its final session, he vowed not to give up his political fight. "I am a stubborn man," he said.
Journalists expressed fear for the future of press freedom under Chinese rule and said self-censorship was spreading like an insidious disease.
"The signs do not seem positive. We hope we are proved wrong," the Hong Kong Journalists Association concluded in a report.
While Hong Kongers made money and politicians bickered, the British military continued its ceremonial retreat from its last stronghold east of Suez.

Kilted soldiers of the Black Watch -- also the last British regiment to bid farewell to the Indian Empire 50 years ago -- repeated their performance against a glorious backdrop encapsulating old and new Hong Kong.
Behind soared the gleaming skyscrapers of this capitalist goldmine, to the left stood the futuristic Convention Centre that will stage the handover to communist-ruled China.
In front was the frigate HMS Chatham, waiting to sail off into the sunset with the troops.
The final inspection complete, the troops marched off into history with a swagger in their step and a lone bagpiper playing.
